facts.text: The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Ankara.

anchor.surface_text: 5.  The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Ankara.

facts.text: In the early hours of 28 April 2005 the applicant went to a primary school in the town of Sincan and poured paint on a statue of Atatürk which was situated in the school’s garden.

anchor.surface_text: 7.  In the early hours of 28 April 2005 the applicant went to a primary school in the town of Sincan and poured paint on a statue of Atatürk[1] which was situated in the school’s garden.

facts.text: On the evening of 28 April 2005, the applicant poured paint on a statue of Atatürk in the garden of another primary school.

anchor.surface_text: 7.  ... On the evening of the same day, he poured paint on a statue of Atatürk in the garden of another primary school.

facts.text: On 6 May 2005 the applicant poured paint on statues of Atatürk in the same two primary schools.

anchor.surface_text: 8.  On 6 May 2005 he did the same thing in the same two primary schools.

facts.text: On 8 July 2005 the applicant poured paint on a statue of Atatürk in Sincan town centre.

anchor.surface_text: 9.  On 8 July 2005 the applicant poured paint on a statue of Atatürk in Sincan town centre.

facts.text: On 12 September 2005 the applicant went to the same statue in Sincan town centre equipped with a tin of paint, paint thinner and a ladder and was arrested by police officers as he was about to open the tin of paint.

anchor.surface_text: 10.  On 12 September 2005 the applicant went to the same statue in Sincan town centre equipped with a tin of paint, paint thinner and a ladder. As he was about to open the tin of paint he was arrested by police officers and taken to a police station where he was questioned.

facts.text: In a statement on 12 September 2005 the applicant told police officers he had carried out the paint pouring actions because he resented Atatürk and expressed his resentment by pouring paint on the statues.

anchor.surface_text: ... In a statement taken from him on the same day the applicant was reported as having told the police officers that he had carried out the above-mentioned actions because he resented Atatürk and had expressed his resentment by pouring paint on the statues.

facts.text: On 12 September 2005 the applicant was brought before a prosecutor and then a judge, who ordered his detention on remand pending criminal proceedings.

anchor.surface_text: 11.  On the same day the applicant was brought before a prosecutor and then a judge, who ordered his detention on remand pending the opening of criminal proceedings against him.

facts.text: In his statement to the prosecutor on 12 September 2005 the applicant said he had carried out his actions to express his “lack of affection” for Atatürk.

anchor.surface_text: In his statement to the prosecutor the applicant maintained that he had carried out his actions to express his “lack of affection” for Atatürk.

facts.text: On 15 September 2005 the Sincan prosecutor charged the applicant with contravening the Law on Offences Committed Against Atatürk (Law no. 5816).

anchor.surface_text: 12.  In his indictment of 15 September 2005, lodged with the Sincan Criminal Court of First Instance (hereinafter “the trial court”), the Sincan prosecutor charged the applicant with the offence of contravening the Law on Offences Committed Against Atatürk (Law no. 5816; see “Relevant Domestic Law and Practice” below).

facts.text: During the trial the applicant admitted pouring paint on the statues and said he was unemployed because the Ministry of Education had not accepted his application to work as a teacher; he committed the offences to protest against that decision.

anchor.surface_text: 13.  In the course of the trial the applicant admitted that he had poured paint on the statues. He told the trial court that he had completed his university studies and qualified as a teacher. However, he had been unemployed for a long time because his application to work as a teacher had not been accepted by the Ministry of Education. He had carried out his offences in order to protest against the Ministry’s decision.

facts.text: On 10 October 2005 the trial court found the applicant guilty and sentenced him to 22 years and 6 months’ imprisonment, considering the offence was committed in public on multiple occasions and increasing the sentence accordingly.

anchor.surface_text: 14.  On 10 October 2005 the trial court found the applicant guilty as charged. Having regard to the fact that the offence was committed in a public place and on a number of occasions, the trial court sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment instead of the minimum term of imprisonment applicable under Law no. 5816, which is one year. The fact that the offence had been committed in a public place also led the trial court to increase the sentence by half in accordance with section 2 of Law no. 5816. The trial court also considered that the applicant had committed the offence on five separate occasions, and decided to multiply the sentence by five. The applicant was thus sentenced to a total prison term of twenty-two years and six months for his above-mentioned actions.

facts.text: The applicant appealed arguing that only one sentence should have been imposed as the five actions constituted one offence, and challenged the trial court’s sentence increases.

anchor.surface_text:
15.  The applicant appealed. In his appeal he argued that, according to the provisions of the Criminal Code, only one sentence should have been imposed on him because, regardless of the fact that he had poured paint on the statues on five occasions, he had in fact only committed one offence and not multiple offences. In support of his argument, he submitted that his five actions had been carried out within a short span of time.

16.  The applicant also pointed out that, instead of imposing on him the minimum one-year prison sentence provided for in Law no. 5816 in respect of each offence, the trial court had handed down a three-year sentence because it had had regard to the number of times he had poured paint on the statues. The trial court had then gone on to rely on the frequency of his actions when multiplying the sentence by five.

17.  The applicant also challenged the trial court’s reliance on section 2 of Law no. 5816 when increasing his sentence by half because the offence had been committed in a public place. He drew the Court of Cassation’s attention to the fact that, by their nature, statues are placed in public places.

facts.text: The applicant maintained he had expressed his “lack of affection” for Atatürk and thus exercised his freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: 18.  The applicant added that he had carried out his actions in order to express his “lack of affection” for Atatürk. As such, he had remained within the boundaries of his right to freedom of expression, which was guaranteed by Article 10 of the Convention.

facts.text: On 6 April 2006 the Court of Cassation rejected the applicant’s freedom of expression argument but quashed the trial court’s judgment for failure to consider that the five incidents could form one offence.

anchor.surface_text: 19.  On 6 April 2006 the Court of Cassation rejected the applicant’s argument that he had been expressing his opinion, but quashed the trial court’s judgment on the ground of, inter alia, that court’s failure to give adequate consideration to the possibility that the five separate incidents could form only one offence and not multiple offences.

facts.text: The Court of Cassation considered the applicant had acted to protest against the Ministry of Education’s decision not to appoint him as a teacher and sent the case back to the trial court.

anchor.surface_text: The Court of Cassation considered that the applicant had carried out his actions in order to protest against the Ministry of Education’s decision not to appoint him as a teacher. The case file was sent back to the trial court.

facts.text: On 5 July 2006 the trial court held the applicant’s actions amounted to a single offence and sentenced him to 13 years, 1 month and 15 days’ imprisonment, the maximum under Law no. 5816, increased by half for public place and by three quarters under Article 43 of the Criminal Code.

anchor.surface_text: 20.  In its decision of 5 July 2006 the trial court agreed with the Court of Cassation’s conclusion, and held that the applicant’s actions had amounted to a single offence and not five offences. However, having regard, inter alia, to the “contradictory reasons” put forward by the applicant as justification for his actions, as well as “the effects of his actions on the public”, the trial court concluded that the applicant’s actions had amounted to “insults”, and deemed it fit to sentence him to five years’ imprisonment, which is the maximum allowed under Law no. 5816. The sentence was then increased by half because the acts had been committed in a public place. Furthermore, pursuant to Article 43 of the Criminal Code (see “Relevant Domestic Law and Practice” below), the sentence was further increased by three quarters. The applicant was thus sentenced to a total of thirteen years, one month and fifteen days’ imprisonment.

facts.text: The trial court set restrictions under section 53 of the Criminal Code banning the applicant from voting, taking part in elections, and running associations, parties, trade unions and cooperatives until execution of his sentence.

anchor.surface_text: 21.  Furthermore, in its decision the trial court set out the restrictions under section 53 of the Criminal Code which were to be placed on the applicant on account of his conviction. Accordingly, until the execution of his sentence, the applicant was banned from, among other things, voting and taking part in elections, as well as from running associations, parties, trade unions and cooperatives (see “Relevant Domestic Law and Practice”).

facts.text: The applicant appealed and repeated his arguments including that he had expressed his “lack of affection” for Atatürk and exercised his freedom of expression under Article 10.

anchor.surface_text: 22.  The applicant appealed and repeated his arguments under various provisions of the Convention. He maintained, in particular, that he had carried out his actions in order to express his “lack of affection” for Atatürk and had thus exercised his freedom of expression guaranteed in Article 10 of the Convention.

facts.text: On 5 February 2007 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal without mentioning his freedom of expression arguments.

anchor.surface_text: 23.  The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on 5 February 2007. No mention was made in the Court of Cassation’s decision of the arguments raised by the applicant about his freedom of expression.

facts.text: On 16 April 2007 a prosecutor set the applicant’s release date as 22 October 2018, with possible early release on 7 June 2014 for good behaviour.

anchor.surface_text: 24.  According to a document drawn up by the prosecutor on 16 April 2007 setting out the details of the applicant’s prison sentence, the date of the applicant’s release from prison was set as 22 October 2018, with a possibility of release on 7 June 2014 for good behaviour.

facts.text: On 1 June 2005 the Law on the Execution of Prison Sentences and Other Security Measures (Law no. 5275) entered into force, setting conditions for early release of prisoners.

anchor.surface_text: 25.  In the meantime, on 1 June 2005 the Law on the Execution of Prison Sentences and Other Security Measures (Law no. 5275) entered into force. This law sets out the circumstances in which prisoners can benefit from early release.

facts.text: On 15 May 2007 the prison prosecutor asked the trial court for guidance on calculating the applicant’s possible early release date, noting different laws applied to offences before and after 1 June 2005.

anchor.surface_text: 26.  On 15 May 2007 the prosecutor responsible for the prison the applicant was serving his sentence in wrote to the trial court and asked for guidance in calculating the date of the applicant’s possible early release. The prosecutor stated that, for offences committed before 1 June 2005, Law no. 647 was applicable and, for offences committed after that date, the new Law no. 5275 would be applicable. The applicant had carried out his actions both before and after that date.

facts.text: On 16 May 2007 the trial court decided the new law was applicable based on the date of the final act.

anchor.surface_text: 27.  On 16 May 2007 the trial court considered that the critical date was the date of the commission of the final act and thus the new law was applicable.

facts.text: The applicant objected that most actions were before 1 June 2005 and the old law should apply; the trial court rejected this on 18 June 2007 and calculated release date accordingly.

anchor.surface_text: 28.  The applicant lodged an objection against that decision and argued that most of his actions had been carried out before 1 June 2005 and that therefore, when calculating his prison sentence, the old law should be taken into account. If his prison sentence were calculated in accordance with the new law, he would spend four more years in prison. That objection was rejected by the trial court on 18 June 2007 and the date of the applicant’s possible release from prison was calculated in accordance with the document drawn up by the prosecutor on 16 April 2007 (see paragraph 24 above).

facts.text: Requests by the applicant to quash his conviction and to rectify the Court of Cassation judgment were rejected on 28 September 2007 and 28 December 2007 respectively.

anchor.surface_text: 29.  A request made by the applicant to the Ministry of Justice for his conviction to be quashed and another request to the Court of Cassation to rectify the judgment were rejected on 28 September 2007 and 28 December 2007 respectively.

facts.text: On 11 June 2013 the applicant was released conditionally.

arguments.claim: The applicant argued that he had carried out his actions with a view to expressing his dissatisfaction with those running the country in accordance with the Kemalist ideology, and to criticising the Kemalist ideology itself.

anchor.surface_text: 40.�The applicant argued that he had carried out his actions with a view to expressing his dissatisfaction with those running the country in accordance with the Kemalist ideology[2], and to criticising the Kemalist ideology itself.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court concluded that the applicant's actions constituted expression within Article 10 and that the provision was applicable.

arguments.claim: The Government considered that defiling Atatürk’s statues was an act of vandalism with the element of insulting Atatürk’s memory and that the law did not prevent criticism of Atatürk's personality or ideas but punished insulting his memory or vandalism.

anchor.surface_text: 41.�The Government considered that defiling Atatürk’s statues was considered to be an act of vandalism with the element of insulting Atatürk’s memory. By virtue of the nation’s deep sense of respect and adoration for Atatürk, his memory was protected by law.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that the applicant's actions were expressive conduct and thus protected by Article 10, rejecting the Government's narrow interpretation.

arguments.claim: The Government argued that it was not the expression of views that was punishable but insulting Atatürk’s memory or vandalising his statues, and that vandalising statues was not a legitimate way of expressing views under Article 10.

anchor.surface_text: 42.�In the opinion of the Government, it was not the expression of views that was punishable under the Law on Offences Committed Against Atatürk, but, rather, insulting Atatürk’s memory or vandalising his statues. That law did not prevent individuals from criticising the personality or ideas of Atatürk or Kemalist policies. Vandalising Atatürk’s statues was not a legitimate way of expressing views under Article 10 of the Convention.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court held that the applicant's conduct was expressive and thus within the scope of Article 10, rejecting the Government's argument.

arguments.claim: The Government argued that the applicant’s unlawful actions had fallen outside the scope of freedom of expression guaranteed by Article 10 because he chose vandalism rather than peaceful expression.

anchor.surface_text: 43.�Having regard to its intensity, the applicant’s aggression against the statues had been qualified as vandalism and vandalism was a violent way of expressing hatred. Although the applicant had the right to express and disseminate his thoughts and opinions through speech, writing, pictures and other media without recourse to violence, he had chosen not to do so. Instead, in order to justify his acts of vandalism the applicant had sought legal protection before the national courts by invoking his right to freedom of expression. In the opinion of the Government, the applicant’s unlawful actions had fallen outside the scope of freedom of expression guaranteed by Article 10 of the Convention.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court rejected the Government's argument that the applicant's conduct was not protected expression, emphasizing the broad scope of Article 10.

arguments.claim: The Court held that Article 10 protects not only the substance of ideas but also the form in which they are conveyed, including artistic expression, symbols, and conduct, and that the applicant's actions constituted expression within Article 10.

anchor.surface_text: 44.�The Court reiterates that Article 10 of the Convention protects not only the substance of the ideas and information expressed, but also the form in which they are conveyed (see Oberschlick v. Austria (no. 1), 23 May 1991, § 57, Series A no. 204). Indeed, a review of the Court’s case-law shows that Article 10 of the Convention has been held to be applicable not only to the more common forms of expression such as speeches and written texts, but also to other and less obvious media through which people sometimes choose to convey their opinions, messages, ideas and criticisms.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court relied on its established case-law recognizing various forms of expression as protected under Article 10.

arguments.claim: The applicant’s conviction, prison sentence and disenfranchisement constituted an interference with his rights under Article 10 § 1 of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: 56.�In light of the foregoing the Court concludes that through his actions the applicant exercised his right to freedom of expression within the meaning of Article 10 of the Convention and that that provision is thus applicable in the present case. It also finds that the applicant’s conviction, the imposition on him of a prison sentence and his disenfranchisement as a result of that conviction constituted an interference with his rights enshrined in Article 10 § 1 of the Convention.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the applicant's conduct to be expression and that the conviction and punishment interfered with Article 10 rights.

arguments.claim: The applicant complained that his actions had been severely and disproportionately penalised and his right to freedom of expression had thus been breached.

anchor.surface_text: 57.�The applicant complained that his actions had been severely and disproportionately penalised and his right to freedom of expression had thus been breached.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted the complaint and found a violation due to disproportionate punishment.

arguments.claim: The Government did not argue that the interference with the applicant’s rights was justified within the meaning of Article 10.

anchor.surface_text: 58.�The Government, beyond disputing the applicability of Article 10 of the Convention, did not seek to argue that the interference had been justified within the meaning of Article 10 of the Convention.

arguments.claim: The restriction on the applicant’s freedom of expression was based on the Law on Offences against Atatürk, which is sufficiently clear and meets foreseeability requirements; the interference was prescribed by law and pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the reputation or rights of others.

anchor.surface_text: 59-60.�The Court observes that the restriction on the applicant’s freedom of expression was based on the Law on Offences against Atatürk. As can be seen from its relevant provisions (see paragraph 31 above), it is sufficiently clear and meets the requirements of foreseeability. The Court is therefore satisfied that the interference was prescribed by law. Moreover, it considers that it can be seen as having pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the reputation or rights of others (see Odabaşı and Koçak v. Turkey, no. 50959/99, § 18, 21 February 2006; see also Dilipak and Karakaya v. Turkey, nos. 7942/05 and 24838/05, §§ 117, 130-131, 4 March 2014).

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the interference was prescribed by law and pursued a legitimate aim.

arguments.claim: Every formality, condition, restriction or penalty imposed in the sphere of freedom of expression must be proportionate to the legitimate aim pursued.

anchor.surface_text: 62.�This means, amongst other things, that every “formality”, “condition”, “restriction” or “penalty” imposed in this sphere must be proportionate to the legitimate aim pursued (ibid.).

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court reiterated the principle of proportionality in restrictions on freedom of expression.

arguments.claim: The Court is struck by the extreme severity of the penalty foreseen in domestic law and imposed on the applicant, over thirteen years imprisonment, which is disproportionate to the offence and not justified.

anchor.surface_text: 66.�Nevertheless, the Court is struck by the extreme severity of the penalty foreseen in domestic law and imposed on the applicant, that is over thirteen years of imprisonment. It also notes that as a result of that conviction the applicant has been unable to vote for over eleven years. In principle, the Court considers that peaceful and non-violent forms of expression should not be made subject to the threat of imposition of a custodial sentence (see, mutatis mutandis, Akgöl and Göl v. Turkey, nos. 28495/06 and 28516/06, § 43, 17 May 2011). While in the present case, the applicant’s acts involved a physical attack on property, the Court does not consider that the acts were of a gravity justifying a custodial sentence as provided for by the Law on Offences against Atatürk.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the punishment disproportionate given the nature and gravity of the acts and the importance of freedom of expression.

arguments.claim: The Court concludes that the penalties imposed on the applicant were grossly disproportionate to the legitimate aim pursued and were therefore not necessary in a democratic society, constituting a violation of Article 10.

anchor.surface_text: 68.�In the light of the foregoing, the Court concludes that the penalties imposed on the applicant were grossly disproportionate to the legitimate aim pursued and were therefore not “necessary in a democratic society”. There has accordingly been a violation of Article 10 of the Convention.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court held that the interference was not necessary in a democratic society due to disproportionate punishment.

arguments.claim: The applicant complained that his conviction and imprisonment prevented him from voting, violating his right to free elections under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1.

anchor.surface_text: 69.�Relying on Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention the applicant complained about the ban which had been imposed on him by the domestic courts and which prevents him from voting.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the applicant was directly affected by the voting ban and that it violated Article 3 of Protocol No. 1.

arguments.claim: The Government acknowledged the applicant’s right to vote had been restricted but argued the restriction was legitimate and not a blanket ban, applying only to intentional offences and aiming at rehabilitation.

anchor.surface_text: 73-75.�The Government acknowledged that Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 guaranteed individual rights, including the right to vote and to stand for election, and did not contest that the applicant’s right to vote had been restricted in the present case. The Government referred to the Explanatory Report of the Criminal Code where the rationale behind section 53 of the Criminal Code is set out (see Söyler, cited above, § 17), and submitted that the legitimate aim of the restriction was the applicant’s rehabilitation. They maintained that the restriction on the right to vote in Turkey was not a “blanket ban” because the applicable legislation limited the scope of the restriction in accordance with the nature of the offence. Referring to the judgment in the case of Hirst v. the United Kingdom (no. 2) ([GC], no. 74025/01, ECHR 2005‑IX), the Government argued that, unlike the situation in the United Kingdom, the Turkish legislation restricting the right to vote was only applicable to persons who had committed offences intentionally. In the United Kingdom the legislation was applicable to all convicted prisoners detained in prisons, irrespective of the length of their sentence, the nature or gravity of the offence, and their individual circumstances.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the Turkish legislation to be an automatic and indiscriminate restriction incompatible with Article 3 of Protocol No. 1.

arguments.claim: The Court found that the Turkish legislation contains no express provisions categorising offences for disenfranchisement and that the automatic and indiscriminate application of this harsh measure does not fall within any acceptable margin of appreciation.
arguments.court_reasoning: The Court reaffirmed its previous findings on the incompatibility of Turkish disenfranchisement legislation with Article 3 of Protocol No. 1.

arguments.claim: The Court concludes that there has been a violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 on account of the applicant’s disenfranchisement.
arguments.court_reasoning: The Court held the automatic disenfranchisement violated the applicant's rights under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1.

arguments.claim: The applicant complained that imposing the maximum prison sentence and calculating his sentence under a new law violated his rights under Articles 5, 6 and 7, that Law no. 5816 gave judges too wide discretion violating Article 14, and that the ban on voting and association violated Article 11.
arguments.court_reasoning: The Court considered it unnecessary to examine these complaints given findings under Articles 10 and 3 of Protocol No. 1.

arguments.claim: The Court rejected the applicant’s claim for pecuniary damage due to lack of evidence but awarded non-pecuniary damage of EUR 26,000.

anchor.surface_text: 84-86.�The applicant claimed 60,000 euros (EUR) in respect of pecuniary damage and EUR 65,000 in respect of non-pecuniary damage. In calculating his claim for pecuniary damage the applicant relied on the minimum wage and multiplied it by the total number of months he was sentenced to serve in prison. The Government argued that the applicant’s claims were excessive and unsupported by evidence. Having regard to the applicant’s failure to submit to the Court any documents showing his employment status, income and loss of income, the Court rejects the applicant’s claim for pecuniary damage. On the other hand, it awards the applicant EUR 26,000 in respect of non-pecuniary damage.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no evidence for pecuniary damage but awarded non-pecuniary damages for suffering.

arguments.claim: Judge Sajó argued that the Court's use of the standard three-step proportionality analysis was inappropriate in this case and that the fundamental issue was the permissibility of sanctioning insults to Atatürk's memory, which is content-based discrimination and incompatible with freedom of expression.

anchor.surface_text: A three-step standard proportionality analysis (the interference is prescribed by law, serves a legitimate aim, and is proportionate to the legitimate aims pursued) is the hallmark of this Courts judgments in Article 8-11 cases... The legislatures predominant concerns in Law no. 5816 are with the content of the speech as opposed to its secondary effects; it expresses the legislatures disagreement with the message the act conveys... A categorical approach is used against applicants, but not against States, in the Article 17 context (see Garaudy v. France (dec.), no. 65831/01, ECHR 20039)... Where disrespect for the memory of a political figure is punished, this has a chilling effect on all speakers.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted the violation of Article 10 but did not explicitly address the deeper content discrimination and chilling effect issues raised by Judge Sajó.
